questions.text: Why pass i as an argument to an outer function inside for (var i)?
options: The parameter receives this iteration’s i. The inner function closes over the parameter, not the loop variable
To stop the loop on this iteration
So that i no longer increments

questions.text: Why are two let declarations with the same name in adjacent case clauses without their own braces an error?
options: Each case is its own scope, but let is forbidden in a case
Both cases sit in the one switch block. Duplicate let names there are a SyntaxError
switch runs twice and the second let overwrites the first
let in a case is hoisted like var

questions.text: Where does n = 2 write inside a nested function if that function does not declare n, but an outer let n exists?
options: To that same outer let. The name is resolved by walking the scope chain outward
It creates a local var of that function

questions.text: Where is a function declared inside a block visible in strict mode?
options: Throughout the outer function, like var
Inside the block and in the next block at the same level

questions.text: A parameter default can read the previous parameter.
The loop for (const i = 0; i < 1; i += 1) increments i and finishes without an error.
If a parameter default reads the next parameter, the call throws ReferenceError.
A var with the same name as a simple parameter resets the argument to undefined at the start of the body.
Why does let n = n throw?
questions.answer: The right-hand side reads the same binding, which is not initialized yet. That is a ReferenceError from the temporal dead zone.

questions.text: Where does an assignment to an undeclared name go in non-strict code?
questions.answer: To a property of the global object. No local variable is created.

questions.text: What remains in an outer let after a block that declares its own let with the same name?
questions.answer: The previous value. The inner let hides the outer one only inside the block and does not write to it.

questions.text: Does typeof bypass the temporal dead zone of let?
questions.answer: No. typeof on a let name before its initialization throws ReferenceError. It does not return "undefined".
